messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam, a 29-year-old jeweler, had spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone, distributing supplies in a village that came under sudden mortar fire. In the chaos, he was grabbed by a colleague to pull him behind a wall, and a child nearby was screaming. He felt his own heart hammering so hard he thought it might stop. He managed to get out physically unharmed, but that moment never left him.

Back home, working in a quiet jewelry store, Liam found himself unable to shake the feeling that danger was everywhere. He started noticing potential weapons—a pair of shears on a bench, the sharp edge of a display case—and he made sure his stool was always positioned so he could see the entire room. Even when his boss assured him the shop was safe, Liam could not believe it. The vigilance felt necessary, but it drained him. When a customer touched his shoulder unexpectedly one afternoon, he flinched so hard he dropped a tray of rings. The sensation—the sudden, unannounced contact—flooded him with the same raw panic he had felt during the attack, even though he could not picture the scene. He was simply terrified, his pulse pounding, with no clear image attached: the emotion came without the memory.

That somatic trigger—his own racing heart—became a recurring problem. Precisely because his heart would race, he would then be plunged into the full emotional intensity of the trauma, again without warning or imagery. To cope, Liam developed habits he thought would help. He reminded himself it could have been worse—at least he was alive, at least he hadn’t been hit. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts, to push away the fear. But these strategies backfired. The downward comparison only sharpened the memory’s grip, because it made him feel guilty for complaining, which looped back to the helplessness of that day. The positive reframing—insisting everything was fine—made his body tighten further, and that increased his awareness of his own heartbeat, which in turn became another trigger. The more he tried to control his thinking, the more his heart pounded and the more he scanned the environment, scanning for threats. This checking ritual directly fed his sense of threat: he would notice a customer’s large coat and imagine a hidden weapon, or catch the glint of a scissors and feel his stomach drop. He could not trust safety no matter what.

The worst moments came when he heard children crying outside his shop. The sound instantly brought back the full memory—not as a series of images but as a visceral replay: the noise, the smell of dust, the feeling of being grabbed. He would freeze at his bench, the tiny screws blurring in front of him. And because the memory was triggered so suddenly, he would scramble to deploy his strategies again: *Think positive. It could have been worse.* But the memory only came back stronger, more real than any ordinary memory. He began to feel that the past was more vivid than the present, which made him doubt the safety of his own daily life.

Over months, Liam became isolated. His relationships suffered because he could not bear to be touched unexpectedly or to hear a child’s cry in a grocery store. At work, he kept his back to the wall and spoke only when necessary. He finally came in for help because he had started feeling the emotion without any trigger at all—just sitting at the bench, his heart would race for no reason, and he would be back inside that war zone, terrified and alone. He wanted the cycle to stop, but he was afraid that if he stopped scanning and checking, something terrible would happen. That was what brought him through the door: exhaustion, a growing sense that his own mind had become the danger, and a desperate hope that he could learn to trust safety again without feeling like he was betraying what he survived.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that the memory itself causes triggers; instead, triggers evoke the memory.
The vignette does not demonstrate that a sense of threat directly leads to the trauma memory; the memory is triggered by specific cues rather than the general feeling of threat.
